correction.text: Place markers one hundred feet ahead and behind, plus one on the traffic side at least ten feet behind

prompt.text: You measure a tow bar before leaving the driveway. What longest span keeps you within the rule?

rationale.text: The limit keeps the towed vehicle close and controlled, so a longer span breaks the rule

lines.text: Towing and breakdowns demand exact distances
Wide stopped vehicles must warn others early

narration.text: Towing another vehicle and handling a roadside breakdown ask for steady judgment and exact placement. In this session we walk through tow link limits, sway rules, and when warning devices become required. You will learn the order for setting signals and how fire habits protect you. Each step uses plain language and clear distances. Stay with each idea and picture yourself beside the stopped vehicle making safe choices.

lines.text: Tow link may span at most fifteen feet
Chain rope cable needs large red square flag
Never operate trailer that whips dangerously sideways

narration.text: The link between towing and towed vehicles may not be longer than fifteen feet from one vehicle to the other. When that link is a chain, rope, or cable, a red flag or other signal at least twelve inches square must be fixed to the connection. A driver must not operate a combination when any towed trailer or vehicle whips or swerves dangerously from side to side. Short links stay easier to control and flags make the link visible. A swaying trailer must be stopped, not driven through.

lines.text: Wide or long stopped vehicle needs warning devices
Legally parked loading or obeying officer excused
Bright light revealing vehicles far excuses devices

narration.text: Warning devices must be shown when a disabled or stopped vehicle at least eighty inches wide or thirty feet long stays on the road for more than ten minutes. They are not required when legally parked in an urban district, lawfully loading passengers, stopped to avoid a conflict, or obeying an officer or traffic control device. Devices may also be omitted when enough light makes people and vehicles visible from one thousand feet away. These triggers focus warnings on longer stops that block the road.

lines.text: Hundred feet ahead behind plus ten feet traffic side
One way rear flag goes two hundred feet back

narration.text: Many learners mix the close traffic side spot with the farther markers, and that trap costs clarity. After the first signal, place flares, electric lights, or reflectors one hundred feet ahead and behind the vehicle, plus one device on the traffic side at least ten feet behind the vehicle. On a one-way street, the rear warning flag must instead be set two hundred feet behind the stopped vehicle. Keep the ten foot close device separate from the hundred foot markers and the one-way exception.

lines.text: First signal beside vehicle facing oncoming traffic
Blocked view pushes device outward within limits
Devices centered in lane or near shoulder

narration.text: In an emergency, first set a flare, lighted fuse, electric lantern, or emergency reflector beside the vehicle on the side facing nearest oncoming traffic. When a breakdown happens within five hundred feet before a curve, hilltop, or other blocked view, the device on that side must be moved farther out, staying between one hundred feet and five hundred feet from the vehicle. Every device must sit in the middle of the occupied lane, or on the shoulder as close as possible to the roadway when fully off the road. Order and position give drivers time to react.

lines.text: Measure the tow link before you drive
Recall the longest allowed span today

narration.text: Here is a quick check: picture your tow bar stretched between two cars in the driveway and ask what longest span keeps you within the rule. The answer is no more than fifteen feet from one vehicle to the other, with a chain, rope, or cable marked by a large red square flag. That short span keeps control and visibility. Hold that number and use it each time you check a tow connection before moving.

lines.text: Keep burning flares from face and fuel
Aim extinguisher bursts wind behind no water

narration.text: You now carry the core roadside family: short flagged steady towing, clear warning triggers, ordered placement, and careful fire response. Keep a burning fuse or flare away from face and eyes, never fasten it to the vehicle, and keep it away from spilled fuel. Prevent tire fires by watching heat and brakes, and fight other fires by aiming bursts carefully with wind at your back, never using water on gasoline or oil. Review placement distances and flare safety before the next practice.

why_how.text: A short tow link keeps the towed vehicle close and controlled, which is why the span may not exceed fifteen feet
A wide or long vehicle stopped over ten minutes blocks the road longer, which is why warning devices become required
Water spreads gasoline and oil rather than smothering them, which is why water must never be used on those fires

Long stops call for clear warnings

narration.text: This short reinforcement session sharpens the pairs learners often swap: link length against flag size, and warning triggers against placement spots. We revisit the fifteen foot tow limit, the red square flag, sway bans, and when a wide or long stop needs devices. You will also lock the close traffic side position and safe flare handling. Listen for exact numbers and picture each roadside choice. These details carry directly into flashcards and practice.

lines.text: Tow link spans at most fifteen feet
Chain rope cable carries red square flag
Never pull trailer whipping dangerously sideways

narration.text: A tow link between vehicles may span at most fifteen feet from one vehicle to the other. A chain, rope, or cable tow link must carry a red flag at least twelve inches square fixed to the connection. A driver must not pull a trailer that whips or swerves dangerously from side to side. Link length limits closeness, the flag marks flexible links, and the sway ban stops an unstable combination. Check all three before any tow begins on a public road.

lines.text: Fifteen feet is span not flag size
Twelve inches square is flag not span

narration.text: The classic trap here swaps fifteen feet with twelve inches, so slow down and sort them. Fifteen feet caps the tow link span from one vehicle to the other, while twelve inches square sizes the red flag on a chain, rope, or cable link. One number controls how far apart vehicles may be, and the other controls how visible a flexible link must be. Naming which number answers which question keeps recall clean under test pressure and at the roadside.

lines.text: Wide long stop over ten minutes warns
Traffic side device ten feet behind
Never fasten lighted flare to vehicle

narration.text: A wide or long disabled vehicle stopped over ten minutes must display warning devices. Keep a traffic side device at least ten feet behind the stopped vehicle as the close guard, with farther markers giving earlier notice. Never fasten a lighted flare or fuse to the vehicle itself, and keep burning devices away from face and spilled fuel. Together these habits warn approaching drivers while keeping the helper safe around heat and flame.

lines.text: Recall the close traffic side spot
State distance behind the stopped vehicle

narration.text: Here is a quick check: after your distant markers are out, where does the close device on the traffic side belong. The answer is on the traffic side at least ten feet behind the stopped vehicle. That close guard protects the exposed edge while farther signals slow traffic early. Say the side and the distance together so the placement stays firm during review and on the road.

lines.text: Refuse swaying trailers every time
Handle flares away from vehicle fuel

narration.text: You reinforced the handoff cluster: short flagged steady towing, clear warning triggers, and safe flare handling. A fifteen foot maximum keeps the link tight, a twelve inch red flag marks chain links, and a whipping trailer must not be pulled. Long wide stops earn devices, the close device stays ten feet back on the traffic side, and burning flares never attach to the vehicle. Carry these pairings into flashcards and the module quiz.

Attaching flame to the vehicle spreads fire to fuel and paint, which is why a lighted flare must never be fastened there

result.text: The close device waits on the traffic side at least ten feet behind the vehicle while farther markers warn earlier
